name: Hard mewing

lead: Hard mewing is a stronger version of mewing: instead of lightly resting the tongue on the palate, the person presses upward with deliberate effort. People use it hoping for a wider, more defined lower face, a more forward midface and better breathing and posture.

The reasoning extends the orthotropic idea that tongue pressure guides upper-jaw growth, with firmer pressure expected to do more. Bone does adapt to strain in general, but no published study has measured what forceful tongue pressure does to the adult face. Forum users most often report wider masseter muscles and a changed look to the cheeks.

paras: Users treat it as a step up from ordinary mewing, done in sessions or held through the day, and often combine it with chewing, chin tucks, thumb pulling or palate expanders. Reports of visible change in photos vary from weeks to years.

Forum users report enlarged masseters, altered cheek appearance, jaw or tongue fatigue, and a gap between the front teeth when combined with thumb pulling and expanders. These are anecdotal accounts; no clinical data exist on forceful tongue pressure, and orthodontic bodies note mewing in general has no supporting trials.

angle.text: Hard mewing is a forceful form of tongue posture used for faster jaw and midface definition, often alongside chewing, thumb pulling and expanders. Posters report wider masseters, which is a muscle change; bone change from tongue pressure has not been studied.

lead: Hard mewing is a looksmaxxing term for a forceful version of mewing: pressing the whole tongue upward against the roof of the mouth with deliberate effort, rather than letting it rest there lightly.[1][2] The goal people state is a better-defined face, with a more forward upper jaw, a sharper jawline, hollower cheeks and a straighter head and neck posture, achieved without surgery.[3] Users treat it as the intensified stage of ordinary mewing and often pair it with chin tucks, chewing, thumb pulling and palate expansion.[4]

Mewing takes its name from British orthodontist John Mew (1928 to 2025), who developed orthotropics, a system that holds facial growth can be guided by tongue and lip posture and by wide dental arches, and from his son Mike Mew, who popularised the practice online.[5] Mew summarised the posture as standing up straight and shutting your mouth. The term "hard mewing" is community vocabulary rather than an orthotropic term, and the posts that use it describe pressing harder and holding the position for long periods.[1][6][7]

No published study has tested hard mewing. Research on the wider orthotropic approach is limited to a 2007 twin study of professionally delivered treatment and commentary papers, and orthodontic bodies, including the American Association of Orthodontists, state there is no evidence mewing improves the jaw.[8]

paras: In forum usage, hard mewing means pushing the tongue firmly into the roof of the mouth, usually with the lips sealed and the teeth lightly together, in contrast to a relaxed resting posture.[1] Some users describe doing it continuously through the day and keeping a multi-year log of the habit.[9][10] One thread frames the distinction directly as "mewing vs hard mewing," with disagreement over whether the extra force adds anything.[1]

Orthotropic teaching, as summarised by Wikipedia, centres on a closed mouth, nasal breathing and a tongue resting against the palate, not on pressing hard.[8] Forum posters who promote hard mewing often justify it by saying more force produces more bone stimulation.[3][7]

John Mew, born in Royal Tunbridge Wells in 1928, qualified in dentistry in 1953 and later trained in orthognathic surgery. In 1958 he proposed the "Tropic Premise," the idea that malocclusion is a postural deformity largely driven by environment rather than genetics, which early intervention could prevent. His orthotropic methods included palatal expanders, dietary changes and training the tongue to rest against the palate. In a 1992 paper he proposed that tongue posture and a firm tongue-to-palate swallow influence oropharyngeal development and ear health, an idea he described as drawn from earlier hypotheses.

The practice reached a large audience in 2019. Google Trends data shows interest in the term rising from January 2019, The Guardian covered it as a YouTube craze in March 2019, and the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery published a commentary that year titled "Mewing: Social Media's Alternative to Orthognathic Surgery?"[8]

Within looksmaxxing forums the practice split into a gentle posture and a "hard" version, and hard mewing appears in threads including long-term progress journals and "why you should start hard mewing" posts.[9][7][10] A 2025 sociological analysis of 8,072 comments in a large looksmaxxing community described how members are encouraged to alter their bodies substantially, citing mewing as an example.

Proponents say that tongue pressure on the palate acts as a natural palate expander, widening and advancing the maxilla, which in turn lifts the cheekbones, opens the airway and raises the lower jaw's position. Hard mewing extends that logic: more force or longer duration should mean more remodelling.[3][7] Some say it works best during growth and post results at ages 14 to 17, while others say it continues to help after puberty.[3]

Posters also say it fixes posture. One user credits hard mewing combined with chin tucks for improved neck-muscle stability and head position, while others report hollow cheeks or a more defined jawline.[3][11] A smaller strand claims benefits for breathing and, following Mew's own writing, for ear and airway health.

Hard mewing is rarely done alone in the threads that describe it. One forum routine lists it with chewing gum, thumb pulling, belt pulling, bonesmashing and chin tucking as part of a daily regimen, and others combine it with maxillary expansion or a palatal expander.[4] Threads on the topic also ask whether a given user's overbite or recessed jaw changes how mewing should be done.[11]

Users disagree about its value. Some posters call hard mewing a decisive tool, one claiming it did more for them than hormones; others ask for photographic proof or title threads "stop hard mewing."[3][12][13] A thread asking what others think of hard mewing shows the same split.[13]

Wikipedia describes mewing as an unproven oral-posture practice, reports that no credible research has shown orthotropics works, and states that most orthodontists do not regard it as an alternative to orthognathic surgery.[8] The American Association of Orthodontists has said there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw.[8]

The research that exists concerns orthotropic treatment by trained practitioners, not self-directed hard mewing. A 2007 study compared 12 sets of identical twins, one twin treated with traditional fixed appliances and the other with orthotropic growth-guidance treatment, and judged outcomes 10 years later using a panel of 12 lay judges, who rated most orthotropically treated twins as improved and most conventionally treated twins as less attractive; the authors reported little difference in dental results and more relapse in the conventional group. A 2019 commentary examined mewing as a social-media alternative to jaw surgery, and a 2026 Journal of Clinical Orthodontics article discusses the mewing trend.

Mechanical-loading research shows bone adapts to strain, and the masseter enlarges in people who clench, grind or chew heavily.[14] No study measures what forceful tongue pressure does to the adult facial skeleton or masseter.

Users report wider masseters, changes in how their cheeks appear and difficulty resting the teeth together after starting hard mewing.[11] A thread describes a gap between the front teeth after combining palatal expansion, thumb pulling and hard mewing, and Wikipedia lists a gap between upper front teeth as a known side effect of palatal expansion, which uses appliances rather than tongue pressure.[15][16]

The documented harm in the mewing story concerns clinical orthotropics. Wikipedia reports that Mike Mew faced a General Dental Council misconduct hearing over harm to child patients, that The Guardian reported on the tribunal on 14 November 2022, that the BBC reported in April 2023 on a treated boy with seizure-like episodes, and that he was struck from the UK dental register in 2024.[8] John Mew's licence was revoked in 2017 over false advertising and breaching patient confidentiality, after a 2010 reprimand.

No studies found. No clinical study has examined forceful tongue pressure on the palate for facial appearance. The wider topic of mewing and orthotropics has one small twin study of professionally delivered orthotropic treatment and commentary articles, none of which tests hard mewing.

On looksmax.org, hard mewing is both promoted and disputed. One poster claimed it gave forward growth even after puberty when combined with chin tucks and sprinting, calling it more effective than drugs, while replies asked for photographic evidence.[3] Another thread describes a user who began hard mewing and noticed wider masseters, hollower cheeks and a harder time resting the teeth together, and asked whether an overbite was responsible.[11] A third user lists hard mewing, chewing, thumb pulling, belt pulling, bonesmashing and chin tucking as parts of a daily regimen.[4] A further thread asks what to do about a gap between the front teeth after palate expansion, thumb pulling and hard mewing.[15]

The discussion shows the belief that more force means more effect, and an opposing view in other threads that it is unproven or counterproductive; one thread title urges members to stop hard mewing.[12] Mewing broadly also entered mainstream media as a meme, with The Independent reporting in March 2024 on students mewing in class.[8]

lore.intro: Hard mewing appears on looksmax.org as the intensive version of mewing, usually in routines with other bone-related practices, with both enthusiasts and sceptics posting threads.[2][4][12]
